swap-story.blurb: Good for lights out, a kid who loves to interrupt, and a parent who only has to keep talking.
steps: Start a made up story, and agree that a tap on the nose means the other person takes over mid sentence.
Whoever gets tapped carries on from the exact word where the story stopped.
Tap more often as you go, until you are swapping every few words.

sock-hunt.title: Sock Hunt
sock-hunt.blurb: Good for a messy sock drawer, a kid of four and up who loves to seek, and a parent who hides sitting down.
steps: Roll five socks into balls and hide them while your kid counts to twenty with eyes shut.
Say "warm" or "cold" as they search, and count the finds out loud.
Swap, so your kid hides and you hunt from your chair with their clues.

mirror.title: Mirror, Mirror
mirror.blurb: Good for a kid who loves being watched and a parent who can stand up but not much more.
steps: Face each other, your kid moves and you copy them as slowly as you can.
Make it harder with faces, then sounds, then silly walks on the spot.
Swap who leads every two minutes, and the leader goes slower each time.

pillow-island.title: Pillow Islands
pillow-island.blurb: Good for a floor full of cushions and a parent who would rather be the lifeguard than swim.
steps: Lay the cushions across the floor as islands, and the floor is the sea.
Your kid crosses the room island to island without touching the water.
Each time they make it across, you take one island away.

simon-says.title: Simon Says
simon-says.blurb: Good for a kid who moves anyway and a parent who can give orders from the sofa.
steps: Call out moves, and your kid only does the ones that start with "Simon says".
Mix in plain orders like "touch your nose" and catch them if they move.
After three catches your kid is Simon and you follow.

bear-dragon.title: Bear and Dragon
bear-dragon.blurb: Good for a kid who adores puppets and a parent with two spare socks and two silly voices.
steps: Put a sock on each hand, one a kind bear with a soft voice and one a grumpy dragon with a growl.
Your kid does whatever the bear asks and never what the dragon orders.
Let the dragon ask for the fun things, like a jump, to make saying no hard.

heads-mean-toes.title: Heads Mean Toes
heads-mean-toes.blurb: Good for a kid of four and up who knows their body parts, and a parent who can call them out from a chair.
steps: Tell your kid that when you say "head" they touch their toes, and when you say "toes" they touch their head.
Call the two words in a random order, slowly at first and then faster.
Add knees and shoulders as a second swapped pair when the first is easy.

purple-light.title: Purple Light
purple-light.blurb: Good for a hallway, a kid who loves to go, and a parent who stands at the finish line.
steps: Stand at one end, and your kid walks toward you on "purple light" and freezes on "red light".
When they reach you, swap the words, so now red means go and purple means stop.
Call the colours faster each round, and whoever wobbles goes back to the start.

sock-colour-freeze.title: Colour Match Freeze
sock-colour-freeze.blurb: Good for one song, a pile of odd socks, and a parent who can hold a sock up from the sofa.
steps: Put on a song, and your kid dances while you hold a handful of different coloured socks.
Stop the music and hold up one sock, so your kid runs to touch something that colour and freezes there.
Start the music again, and the next sock is a new colour.

cup-drum-walk.title: Cup Drum Walk
cup-drum-walk.blurb: Good for a kid who marches anyway and a parent who can tap a spoon on an upturned cup.
steps: Tap a spoon on an upturned cup, and your kid walks one step for every beat, fast or slow as you play.
Change the speed without warning and see how fast their feet catch up.
Now flip it, so fast beats mean slow steps and slow beats mean fast feet.

clap-conductor.title: The Conductor
clap-conductor.blurb: Good for a kid who claps for everything and a parent conducting from the armchair.
steps: Hold your hands high for loud claps and low for soft ones, and your kid claps along.
Close your fist for silence, and open it to start again.
Swap, so your kid conducts with their hands and you clap, obeying every move.

clap-echo.title: Clap Echo
clap-echo.blurb: Good for a kitchen chair, a kid who copies everything, and a parent with just their hands.
steps: Clap a short pattern, and your kid claps it straight back.
Add one clap each round, and mix slow and quick ones.
When they miss, your kid makes the patterns and you echo.

sock-sort-switch.title: Sock Sort Switch
sock-sort-switch.blurb: Good for laundry day, a kid who likes piles, and a parent sorting from the floor.
steps: Tip out the socks, and your kid sorts them by colour onto two cushions, dark here and light there.
Once the pile is gone, mix them up and switch the rule to size, big socks here and small socks there.
Call "switch" halfway through a pile for a real test.

cup-shuffle.title: Cup Shuffle
cup-shuffle.blurb: Good for the kitchen table, a kid of four and up with sharp eyes, and a parent who can slide three cups.
steps: Turn three cups upside down and hide a sock ball under one while your kid watches.
Slide two cups past each other slowly, then swap another pair, and ask which cup hides the sock.
Add a swap each round, then hand over the cups so your kid shuffles and you guess.

build-my-plan.title: Build My Plan
build-my-plan.blurb: Good for a kid who builds and a parent who would rather describe a tower than stack it.
steps: Describe a tower in words first, like three cups, then the book, then two cups on top.
Your kid builds it from memory while you keep your hands in your lap.
Check it together against the plan, then your kid describes one and you build.

five-breath-zoo.title: Five Breath Zoo
five-breath-zoo.blurb: Good for a wound up kid who likes animals and a parent who can stand still.
steps: Pick an animal shape, like a tall giraffe on tiptoes or a frog crouched low, and both of you hold it.
Count five slow breaths out loud while nobody wobbles or talks.
Your kid picks the next animal, and the poses get harder each round.

pretend-restaurant.title: Pretend Restaurant
pretend-restaurant.blurb: Good for a kid who loves to serve and a parent who can sit at a table and be fussy.
steps: Sit down as the customer and order three dishes, like soup, a pizza and a banana.
Your kid the waiter repeats the order back, then cooks it from cushions and cups.
They serve the three dishes in the order you asked, and the next round you add a drink.

opposite-day-preschool.title: Opposite Day
opposite-day-preschool.blurb: Good for a kid who thinks rules are funny and a parent who can call them out from a chair.
steps: Today "walk" means stop and "stop" means walk, so say them and watch your kid do the opposite.
Add "loud" for whispering and "quiet" for shouting.
Whoever gets three right in a row makes up the next pair of opposites.

sculptor-statue.title: Sculptor and Statue
sculptor-statue.blurb: Good for a kid who can stand still for a dare and a parent who moves slowly anyway.
steps: Your kid is the clay, so gently move an arm here and a leg there into a pose.
Walk slowly round your statue pulling faces while it holds perfectly still.
Swap, and your kid sculpts you into something ridiculous.

less-is-more.title: Less Is More
less-is-more.blurb: Good for a kid who always wants the big pile and a parent who can count socks sitting down.
steps: Make two piles of sock balls, one with two socks and one with five.
Tell them the rule, the pile they point to goes to you and the other pile is theirs.
Count what each of you got, then mix the piles and try again.

closed-hands.title: Closed Hands
closed-hands.blurb: Good for a kid who cannot wait and a parent with a small toy in a pocket.
steps: Your kid shuts their eyes and holds out two closed hands.
Count slowly to twenty together, and if their eyes or hands open you start the count again.
At twenty, a small toy lands in their hands, and next round the count grows by five.

book-detective.title: Book Detective
book-detective.blurb: Good for the sofa, a kid who knows every page, and a parent who can point.
steps: Open any picture book and ask your kid to find something red on the page.
Next ask for something round, then for something that is both red and round.
Swap, so your kid picks the clue and you search.

slow-tightrope.title: Slow Tightrope
slow-tightrope.blurb: Good for a hallway, a kid with good balance, and a parent who claps from the end.
steps: Lay a scarf or towel flat along the floor as the tightrope.
Your kid walks it heel to toe as slowly as they can, and the slowest crossing wins.
Add a sock ball balanced on their head for the next crossing.

whisper-orders.title: Whisper Orders
whisper-orders.blurb: Good for a sleeping sibling, a loud kid, and a parent who is done with noise.
steps: Whisper a silly order in your kid's ear, like hop to the door and back.
They do it and whisper back what they did, and any loud voice costs a turn.
Swap, and your kid whispers the orders.

floor-map.title: Floor Map Journey
floor-map.blurb: Good for a room with cushions, a kid who loves adventures, and a parent who stays at base camp.
steps: The floor is a map, so cushions are mountains, a scarf is a river and the sofa is the castle.
Plan the route out loud together, like river, then mountains, then castle, before anyone moves.
Your kid travels the whole route from memory, then plans a new one for you.

three-moves.title: Three Moves
three-moves.blurb: Good for a kid who copies everything and a parent who can show a move sitting down.
steps: Show three moves in a row, like a jump, a toe touch and a clap.
Your kid does all three in the same order, and if they get it, add a fourth.
Now ask for the same moves backwards.

turtle-rabbit.title: Turtle and Rabbit
turtle-rabbit.blurb: Good for a kitchen table, a kid with a crayon, and a parent who does the voices.
steps: Your kid draws a line across the page as slowly as a turtle while you count.
Say "rabbit" and the line races to the edge, then "turtle" and it crawls again.
Switch animals halfway along a line, and give the turtle a long turn.

my-rule-your-rule.title: My Rule, Your Rule
my-rule-your-rule.blurb: Good for a bossy kid and a parent who does not mind being bossed from a chair.
steps: Make one rule, like every time I clap you hop, and play it for a minute.
Then your kid makes the rule, and you both follow theirs.
For the last round keep both rules at once.

sock-money-shop.title: Sock Money Shop
sock-money-shop.blurb: Good for a kid who loves pretend money and a parent who can run a shop from the sofa.
steps: Line up a few toys on the sofa as the shop, and rolled socks are the coins.
Price each toy at one, two or three socks, and your kid pays by counting coins into your hand.
Swap, and you pay at their shop while they check your counting.

sun-moon-switch.title: Sun and Moon
sun-moon-switch.blurb: Good for a dim evening, a kid who loves the light switch, and a parent standing by it.
steps: Light on means your kid says "night" and curls up, and light off means they say "day" and stretch awake.
Flick the switch at odd moments, slowly at first and then quickly.
Swap, so your kid works the switch and you get it wrong on purpose.

lips-and-ears.title: Lips and Ears
lips-and-ears.blurb: Good for story time, a kid who interrupts, and a parent who can hold a spoon.
steps: The spoon holder is the mouth and talks about the page, and the cup holder is the ear and only listens.
Swap the spoon and cup at every page turn.
The ear repeats one thing the mouth said before the next page.

ready-steady-wait.title: Ready Steady Wait
ready-steady-wait.blurb: Good for a kid who jumps the gun and a parent who can hold a cup on their knees.
steps: Hold a cup on your knees, and your kid stands back with three sock balls to throw in.
They may only throw after you say "go", and your count before it changes every time.
Any throw before "go" comes back to the pile.

under-the-cloth.title: Under the Cloth
under-the-cloth.blurb: Good for a tea towel, a handful of toys, and a parent who can count to ten.
steps: Lay out five small things, let your kid look for a count of ten, then cover them with a cloth.
Your kid names everything under the cloth, then lifts it to check.
Add one thing each round, and swap so you have to remember theirs.

say-not-do.title: Say Not Do
say-not-do.blurb: Good for a kid who watches your hands and a parent who can fib with them from a chair.
steps: Say "touch your nose" while you touch your ear, and your kid must do what you say, not what you do.
Match your words and hands sometimes so they cannot guess.
Swap, and try not to copy their cheating hands.

program-the-robot.title: Program the Robot
program-the-robot.blurb: Good for a kid who likes being in charge and a parent happy to walk very slowly.
steps: You are a robot that only moves on exact orders, like two steps forward or turn left.
Your kid gives three orders at once to steer you to a cup, and you do them in that order.
Bump into a chair when an order is wrong, and ask "what next" instead of fixing it.

silent-zoo.title: Silent Zoo
silent-zoo.blurb: Good for a late evening, a kid who roars, and a parent who guesses from the sofa.
steps: Your kid acts out an animal with their body only, and no sound is allowed.
Guess out loud, and any squeak from the animal means you win the round.
Swap, and act out a dragon brushing its teeth in total silence.

pattern-tower.title: Pattern Tower
pattern-tower.blurb: Good for a tub of blocks or cups and a parent who likes patterns more than mess.
steps: Start a tower with a pattern, like red, blue, red, blue, and say it out loud.
Your kid adds the next block and must keep the pattern going.
Start a trickier pattern next, like big, big, small.

magic-word.title: Magic Word
magic-word.blurb: Good for a bedtime book and a parent who wants the kid listening to every word.
steps: Pick a word that comes up a lot in the book, like "bear", and that is the magic word.
Read aloud, and your kid jumps up every time they hear it and sits straight back down.
Halfway through, change the magic word.

stop-the-song.title: Stop the Song
stop-the-song.blurb: Good for a kid who sings loudly and a parent who can raise one hand.
steps: Sing a song you both know, and your kid sings along.
Raise your hand at any moment and the song stops dead, even in the middle of a word.
Lower your hand to carry on exactly where you left off, then hand the stopping job to your kid.

ten-second-ears.title: Ten Second Ears
ten-second-ears.blurb: Good for a walk home, a chatty kid, and a parent who would love ten seconds of quiet.
steps: Stop, and nobody speaks or moves for a slow count of ten.
Then each of you names three sounds you heard.
Do it again and try to find a sound nobody heard the first time.

topsy-turvy-sort.title: Topsy Turvy Sort
topsy-turvy-sort.blurb: Good for a floor full of toys and a parent who can judge from a chair.
steps: Put a big cushion and a small cushion on the floor and gather a pile of toys.
Big toys go on the small cushion and small toys go on the big one, and no toy touches the wrong one.
Swap the rule back to normal when your kid stops hesitating.

no-repeats-roll.title: No Repeats Roll
no-repeats-roll.blurb: Good for a kid who knows a lot of animals and a parent sitting on the floor with a ball.
steps: Sit facing each other and roll a ball back and forth.
Each roll you say an animal, and nobody may say one that has already been said.
Whoever repeats one picks the next topic, like food or colours.

slow-motion-replay.title: Slow Motion Replay
slow-motion-replay.blurb: Good for a kid who scores goals and a parent who commentates from the sofa.
steps: Your kid kicks a sock ball at the cushion goal and celebrates.
Call "replay" and they do the exact same kick and celebration in slow motion while you commentate.
Ask for the replay even slower, and then one where the ball is caught.

teach-your-teddy.title: Teach Your Teddy
teach-your-teddy.blurb: Good for a kid who loves to explain and a parent happy to be the teddy's voice.
steps: Your kid teaches their teddy how to stack five cups, saying each step out loud before doing it.
Be the teddy and ask slow questions like "which cup goes first".
Knock it over gently as the teddy, and ask your kid to teach it again faster.

fill-the-gap.title: Fill the Gap
fill-the-gap.blurb: Good for a bedtime song, a kid of four and up who knows the words, and a parent who can stop singing.
steps: Sing a song you both know and stop right before a word.
Your kid sings the missing word, then you carry on.
Next time stop before two words, then before a whole line.

tap-the-cups.title: Tap the Cups
tap-the-cups.blurb: Good for a table with four cups and a parent who can tap them in order.
steps: Line up four cups and tap two of them in a row while your kid watches.
Your kid taps the same cups in the same order.
Add one tap each round, then swap and try to follow their taps.

step-step-clap.title: Step Step Clap
step-step-clap.blurb: Good for a hallway, a kid who marches, and a parent who can clap the rhythm from a chair.
steps: Show a pattern, step, step, clap, and your kid walks the hallway repeating it.
Call a new pattern as they walk, like step, clap, clap, and they switch on the spot.
Let your kid invent a pattern that you clap out while they walk it.

animal-or-food.title: Animal or Food
animal-or-food.blurb: Good for the back seat or the sofa, and a parent who can think of a lot of nouns.
steps: Say a word, and if it is an animal your kid puts their hands up, and if it is food they pat their knees.
Say them faster and slip in tricky ones like a chocolate bunny.
Swap the moves round after a few rounds, so animals pat and food goes up.

pass-the-pose.title: Pass the Pose
pass-the-pose.blurb: Good for a kid who copies you and a parent who can lift one arm.
steps: Strike a pose, and your kid copies it exactly, then changes one thing, like a raised arm.
Copy their new pose and say what changed before you change one thing yourself.
Keep passing the pose back and forth until it gets ridiculous.

banana-means-yes.title: Banana Means Yes
banana-means-yes.blurb: Good for a car ride, a chatty kid, and a parent who asks a lot of questions anyway.
steps: For this game "banana" means yes and "apple" means no, and nobody may say the real words.
Ask quick questions like "do you like ice cream" and catch any slip.
Swap, and your kid tries to trick you.

peek-and-build.title: Peek and Build
peek-and-build.blurb: Good for a tub of blocks, a kid who builds, and a parent who can hide behind a cushion.
steps: Build a small tower of three blocks behind a cushion where your kid cannot see.
Lift the cushion for a count of five, hide it again, and your kid builds the same tower from memory.
Add a block each round, then swap builders.

what-else-is-it.title: What Else Is It
what-else-is-it.blurb: Good for a kid who pretends everything and a parent with one cup and no energy to fetch more.
steps: Hold up a cup and say "this is a hat" and wear it.
Pass it to your kid, who makes it something new, like a phone or a boat, and shows you.
Nobody may repeat an idea, and the round ends when the cup is finally a cup again.

one-more-hop.title: One More Hop
one-more-hop.blurb: Good for a hallway, five socks, and a parent who can call numbers from the end.
steps: Lay five socks in a line as hopping spots and number them one to five out loud.
Call a number and your kid hops to the spot one more than you said.
When that is easy, switch to one less.

grandma-footsteps.title: Grandma's Footsteps
grandma-footsteps.blurb: Good for a kid who loves to sneak and a parent who can turn round in a chair.
steps: Sit in a chair with your back to your kid, who starts at the far wall.
They creep toward you, and whenever you turn round they must be frozen still.
Anyone you catch moving goes back to the wall, and a tap on your shoulder wins.

empty-cups.title: Empty Cups
empty-cups.blurb: Good for a table, five cups, a kid of four and up, and a parent who can hide three socks.
steps: Turn five cups upside down and hide a sock ball under three of them while your kid looks away.
Your kid lifts one cup at a time to find all three socks, and an empty cup goes back down.
Between lifts they shut their eyes for a count of five, and the goal is fewer lifts than last round.

which-toy.title: Which Toy
which-toy.blurb: Good for a shelf of toys and a parent who can answer yes or no from the sofa.
steps: Line up six toys and pick one in your head without saying it.
Your kid asks yes or no questions, like "is it soft", and pushes aside the toys that are ruled out.
When they name it, swap and you do the asking.

stop-at-seven.title: Stop at Seven
stop-at-seven.blurb: Good for a kid who bounces and a parent who can count out loud from a chair.
steps: Agree a number, like seven, and your kid starts jumping while you count aloud.
They must stop exactly on seven, not before and not after, however loudly you keep counting.
Pick a new number each round, and sometimes count quietly in your head.

just-enough-roll.title: Just Enough Roll
just-enough-roll.blurb: Good for a soft ball, a quiet floor, and a parent sitting against the sofa.
steps: Put a cushion a few steps away and your kid rolls the ball so it just touches it and stops.
Too hard and it rolls past, too soft and it stops short, so they get three tries.
Move the cushion further or closer, then swap and let them judge your roll.

car-clap.title: Car Clap
car-clap.blurb: Good for a traffic jam, a kid in the back seat, and a parent who is not driving.
steps: Your kid claps once for every red car that passes, and never for a white one.
After a few, swap the rule, so now white cars get the clap and red cars get silence.
Add a bus for a stamp of the feet.

oops-plan.title: Oops Plan
oops-plan.blurb: Good for a kid deep in pretend play and a parent who can throw in trouble from a chair.
steps: Your kid says the plan for their game in three parts, like "the bear shops, then cooks, then a party".
Play along, and once in the game you shout "oops" with a problem, like the shop has run out of food.
Your kid says the new plan out loud before the game goes on, and the party still has to happen.

secret-sorter.title: Secret Sorter
secret-sorter.blurb: Good for a heap of toys on the floor and a kid who likes to crack a code.
steps: Put two cushions down and think of a secret rule, like soft toys on the left and hard toys on the right.
Your kid places one toy at a time, and you only say "yes" or "no" until they are getting them all right.
They say the rule out loud, then make up a secret rule of their own for you to crack.

three-zones.title: Three Zones
three-zones.blurb: Good for a kid who will not sit still and a parent who can referee from the sofa.
steps: Give three spots a rule each: on the rug you can only whisper, at the door you hop, on the sofa you sing.
Your kid wanders between the spots and must follow the rule of wherever they are standing.
After a few minutes swap two rules round, so the rug hops and the door whispers.

changing-ball.title: Changing Ball
changing-ball.blurb: Good for two people standing in a kitchen with nothing in their hands.
steps: Pass an invisible ball to your kid and say what it is now, like "heavy as a rock".
They catch it that way, then change it, like "hot as soup" or "light as a feather", and throw it back.
Every throw changes the ball, and whoever forgets how to hold it drops it with a loud splat.

toy-homes.title: Toy Homes
toy-homes.blurb: Good for a room with toys everywhere and a parent sitting in the middle of them.
steps: Pick four toys and give each one a home, like the bear lives on the chair and the car lives under the table.
Pile the toys at your feet, sing one song together, then your kid walks each toy home.
Next round announce that two toys have swapped houses, and they deliver again.

colour-hop.title: Colour Hop
colour-hop.blurb: Good for a hallway, a drawer of odd socks, and a kid with hops to spare.
steps: Lay four different coloured socks in a line along the floor with a gap between each.
Call three colours, like "red, blue, red", and your kid hops onto them in that order.
Make it four colours when three is easy, then your kid calls the colours and you step them.

teddy-tempter.title: Teddy Tempter
teddy-tempter.blurb: Good for a kid who gets pulled off every job and a parent happy to be the pest for once.
steps: Your kid stacks five cups while saying each step out loud, like "now the blue one on top".
You are the teddy beside them, doing anything silly to catch their eye, but never touching the cups.
A look at the teddy wins the teddy the round, and after three rounds you swap jobs.

eyes-on-me-preschool.title: Eyes on Me
eyes-on-me-preschool.blurb: Good for a kid who wants it now, and a parent standing between them and the toy.
steps: Hold a toy they want down by your knee and tell your kid it is theirs after a count of ten.
The rule is their eyes stay on your eyes the whole count, and one glance down starts the ten again.
Hand it over on ten, then let them hold a toy and test you.

flamingo-pass.title: Flamingo Pass
flamingo-pass.blurb: Good for a ball, a bit of floor, and a parent who can stand on one leg for about a minute.
steps: Stand a few steps apart, both on one leg like flamingos, and pass the ball gently back and forth.
If a foot touches the floor, that player counts to five on two feet before lifting one again.
Swap legs after ten passes, then try ten passes with eyes on the ball and no talking.

call-the-stop.title: Call the Stop
call-the-stop.blurb: Good for a ball, a quiet floor, and a parent who can roll from a chair.
steps: Roll the ball gently across the floor and both watch it slow down.
Your kid calls "stop" at the exact moment it stops moving, not a second before and not after.
They roll it back and you call the stop, and the closest call of the night wins.

find-the-song-preschool.title: Find the Song
find-the-song-preschool.blurb: Good for a room with hiding places and a kid of four and up with sharp ears.
steps: Start a quiet song on your phone and hide it in the room while your kid shuts their eyes and hums.
They listen, walk toward the music and find the phone, hands behind their back until they are sure.
Swap over, and turn the song down a notch every round.

stop-and-name.title: Stop and Name
stop-and-name.blurb: Good for a kid who needs to move and a parent who needs to stay exactly where they are.
steps: Your kid walks round the room while you sit and watch.
Call "stop", and they must name the last three things they walked past, in order.
Swap, so they call and you do the walking.

freeze-dance.title: Freeze Dance
freeze-dance.blurb: Good for one song, a wiggly kid, and a parent with one wild dance left in them.
steps: Put on one song and dance as wildly as you can.
Whoever is in charge shouts "Freeze!" at any moment, and everyone holds still.
Anyone who wobbles is in charge next.

animal-race.title: Animal Race
animal-race.blurb: Good for a hallway, loud animals, and a kid who has to run before bed.
steps: Race down the hallway as a crab.
Race back as a frog, then a bear, then a snake.
The winner picks the next animal.

obstacle.title: Obstacle Course
obstacle.blurb: Good for builders, a slow count out loud, and a room you don't mind rearranging.
steps: Build a course that goes under a chair, over a cushion and around the table.
Time your kid with a slow count out loud.
They change one obstacle, then they time you.

three-lights.title: Three Lights
three-lights.blurb: Good for a hallway, a kid who knows red light green light, and one new rule to trip you both.
steps: Stand at one end of the hallway and call "green light" to run and "red light" to stop.
Add "purple light", which means tiptoe, and shout the three in any order.
When your kid reaches you, they call the lights and you do the running.

sleeping-animals.title: Sleeping Animals
sleeping-animals.blurb: Good for a kid who cannot lie still, and a parent who wants ten seconds of quiet first.
steps: Lie on the floor pretending to sleep while you hum "sleeping, sleeping, all the children are sleeping".
Whisper "and when they woke up they were" and name an animal.
Everyone wakes and moves like that animal until you say "sleeping" again.

backwards-dance.title: Backwards Dance
backwards-dance.blurb: Good for a dance party where the rules are upside down and nobody gets it right.
steps: Put on a song and dance to it, fast bits fast and slow bits slow.
Now flip it, so fast music means slow motion and slow music means wild dancing.
Say "switch" to swap the rule back, and keep switching faster each time.

two-orders-go.title: Two Orders, Go
two-orders-go.blurb: Good for a kid who stops listening after one word, and a room with corners to run to.
steps: Give two orders in a row, like "touch the door, then sit on the sofa", and only then say "go".
Your kid runs both in order, and you cheer when the second one is right.
Swap, and make them give you three orders if two were easy.

wiggle-and-stop.title: Wiggle and Stop
wiggle-and-stop.blurb: Good for a kid with the wriggles, a parent who can sing badly, and stops that keep getting longer.
steps: Sing "wiggle your arms, wiggle your arms" and both of you wiggle only that part.
Sing "stop" and hold still, making each stop one count longer than the last.
Name a new part each time, down to just eyebrows.

memory-relay.title: Memory Relay
memory-relay.blurb: Good for a long hallway and a kid who can carry three things in their head if they hurry.
steps: Name three things in the far room, like "a cup, a sock and the blue car", and say "go".
Your kid runs and brings all three back in one trip while you count loudly.
Swap, and they name four things for you to fetch.

clap-swap-leader.title: Clap Swap
clap-swap-leader.blurb: Good for a kid who always wants to be the boss, and a parent happy to be bossed half the time.
steps: March around the room as the leader while your kid copies every move you make.
Anyone can clap once, and on that clap the follower becomes the leader without stopping.
Clap more often as you go, until you swap every few steps.

clap-feet.title: Clap Feet
clap-feet.blurb: Good for stompy feet, a kitchen floor, and a parent who sets the pace with their hands.
steps: Clap slowly and your kid steps once per clap, clap fast and their feet go fast.
Stop clapping and their feet must stop too, even in mid step.
Swap so they clap and you run, and let them trick you with a sudden stop.

sock-toss-count.title: Sock Toss Count
sock-toss-count.blurb: Good for a pile of clean socks, a cup on the floor, and a kid who likes to count out loud.
steps: Set a cup across the room and roll every sock into a ball.
Take turns tossing, counting out loud only the socks that land in, and run to collect the misses.
Each time the cup fills, step one stride further back and start the count again.

plan-then-hide.title: Plan Then Hide
plan-then-hide.blurb: Good for a hide and seek that lasts longer than ten seconds, and a kid who hides in the same place.
steps: Before hiding, the hider says the plan out loud, like "behind the curtain, feet tucked in, no giggling".
The seeker counts to twenty with eyes shut, then hunts while saying out loud what they see.
Swap after every find, and each new plan needs one new idea for staying still.

rescue-mission.title: Rescue Mission
rescue-mission.blurb: Good for a superhero in pyjamas, a toy in trouble, and a parent who can still run a lap.
steps: Put a toy somewhere high or far and tell your kid it needs rescuing.
Together say the plan in three steps, like "crawl under the table, hop the cushions, stretch up the sofa".
Shout "go" and run the plan exactly, then your kid sets up the next rescue.

widening-river.title: Widening River
widening-river.blurb: Good for jumpers, two cushions, and a parent who moves the banks a hand wider every go.
steps: Lay two cushions as river banks, and nobody jumps until the other one says "jump".
After every dry landing, slide the banks one hand apart.
A splash means one crawl lap round the room as a fish before the next go.

knees-mean-toes.title: Knees Mean Toes
knees-mean-toes.blurb: Good for a kid of four and up, a song you both know, and words that stop meaning what they say.
steps: Sing "head, shoulders, knees and toes" and touch each part, then sing it again twice as fast.
Now swap two parts, so "head" means touch your toes and "toes" means touch your head.
Sing it slowly with the swap, then speed up until someone gets tangled.

pillow-tower-wait.title: Pillow Tower Wait
pillow-tower-wait.blurb: Good for a kid who smashes everything, now with a wait before the smash.
steps: Stack every cushion and pillow into a tall wobbly tower.
Your kid stands close with hands behind their back until you say the magic word you both chose.
Say other words first to tempt them, then the magic word, and they crash through it.

clap-parade.title: Clap Parade
clap-parade.blurb: Good for a march round the sofa with four animals your kid has to keep in order.
steps: Agree on four animals in order, like elephant, frog, snake, bird, and say the list twice.
Parade round the room as the first animal, and on every clap everyone switches to the next on the list.
After the bird comes the elephant again, and the one who forgets the order does the clapping next.

sock-in-a-cup.title: Sock in a Cup
sock-in-a-cup.blurb: Good for a hallway, one cup, one sock, and a kid who needs a reason to slow down.
steps: Turn a cup upside down on your flat palm and balance a rolled sock on top.
Walk the hallway and back without dropping the sock, slowly first, then a little faster.
Make it harder with a second sock on top, or by walking it backwards.

yes-means-run.title: Yes Means Run
yes-means-run.blurb: Good for a kid who runs before they listen, and a parent full of silly questions.
steps: Ask a quick question, like "do cows fly?", and your kid runs to the far wall only if the answer is yes.
If the answer is no, they freeze right where they are until the next question.
Ask faster, mix in some tricky ones, and then let them ask you.

full-body-mirror.title: Full Body Mirror
full-body-mirror.blurb: Good for a slow song, a kid who copies everything anyway, and a parent who can move like honey.
steps: Stand facing each other with a slow song on, and you lead with big slow moves of your whole body.
Your kid mirrors you exactly, so when you lift your left arm they lift their right.
Swap leaders when the song ends, and the new leader has to use their feet too.

crocodile-river.title: Crocodile River
crocodile-river.blurb: Good for a floor full of cushions, a snapping parent, and a kid who plans before they leap.
steps: Scatter the cushions as stepping stones across the room, and you crawl between them as the crocodile.
Your kid names their route out loud, like "big one, blue one, flat one", then crosses on exactly those.
Any foot in the water gets a gentle snap, and after each crossing the crocodile removes one stone.

window-spy-run.title: Window Spy Run
window-spy-run.blurb: Good for a grey evening at the window and a kid who needs a reason to sprint across the room.
steps: Stand at the window together and say "I spy something red" about a thing outside.
Your kid points it out, then races to touch something that colour inside before you count to ten.
Swap, and try to catch each other out with colours like brown or white.

conductor-arms.title: Conductor
conductor-arms.blurb: Good for a kid with no volume knob, and a parent who wants to hold the baton for once.
steps: Put a song on and stand as the conductor with your arms as the volume knob.
Arms high means big loud dancing, arms down low means tiny silent moves.
Move your arms slowly, then suddenly, then hand the conducting to your kid.

cup-drum-third-beat.title: Third Beat Freeze
cup-drum-third-beat.blurb: Good for an upturned cup, a dancing kid, and a drummer who hides the beat that counts.
steps: Your kid dances while you drum on an upturned cup, and they must freeze exactly on the third hit.
Space the hits out, slow then quick, so the third one is hard to guess.
Make the fourth hit the new freeze beat once three is easy, then give your kid the cup.

rocket-launch.title: Rocket Launch
rocket-launch.blurb: Good for a kid who cannot wait, a countdown they know, and one giant jump at the end.
steps: Crouch together as rockets and count down from ten, sinking lower on every number.
At zero everyone freezes in silence for three slow breaths, and an early launch means counting down again.
Whisper "blast off" and leap as high as you can, then your kid counts the next one.

shape-freeze.title: Shape Freeze
shape-freeze.blurb: Good for a kid who runs in circles, and a parent who can turn a shout into a tree, a star or a ball.
steps: Your kid runs round the room until you call a shape, like "star", "ball" or "tree".
They freeze as that shape and hold it while you count to five, wobbling allowed, moving not.
Add a new shape every round, like "bridge" or "rock", and keep calling the old ones too.

add-a-move.title: Add a Move
add-a-move.blurb: Good for a growing chain of jumps and hops that gets longer until someone forgets the start.
steps: You do one move, like a jump, and your kid copies it.
They add a second move, and you both do the whole chain from the start.
Keep adding one move each turn, and when the chain breaks, start a fresh one with their move first.

clap-code.title: Clap Code
clap-code.blurb: Good for a secret code of claps and a kid who wants to crack it at full speed.
steps: Agree a code where one clap means jump, two claps mean crouch and three claps mean run to the door.
Clap the codes in any order and your kid does the matching move.
Swap one meaning around once they are good, then let them clap for you.

light-spot-chase-preschool.title: Light Spot Chase
light-spot-chase-preschool.blurb: Good for a dim evening, a phone torch, and a kid who wants to catch something that cannot be caught.
steps: Dim the room, shine your phone torch on the floor, and slide the spot slowly for your kid to stamp on.
Switch the torch off at any moment and your kid freezes, pointing to where the spot was.
Speed the spot up a little each round, then hand your kid the torch and do the stamping.

sorting-sprint.title: Sorting Sprint
sorting-sprint.blurb: Good for a floor covered in toys, two cushions as bins, and a rule that flips halfway.
steps: Pile the toys at one end of the room and put two cushions at the other as the two bins.
Call "colour" and your kid sprints each toy to the red bin or the not red bin, one toy per run.
Call "size" and now big toys go left and small ones right, with the same toys still coming.

lap-then-find.title: Lap Then Find
lap-then-find.blurb: Good for four cushions, one small toy, and a kid of four and up who can hold a secret while they run.
steps: Spread four cushions round the room and hide a toy under one while your kid watches.
They run one full lap of the room, then go straight to the right cushion.
Add one more lap each round, and swap so you have to remember while you run.

safe-spot-lava.title: Safe Spot Lava
safe-spot-lava.blurb: Good for a room with a sofa, a rug and cushions, when the floor has just turned into lava.
steps: Name one safe thing, like "the rug", and everyone walks about until you shout "lava".
On "lava" you both have five counts to get onto the safe thing, no touching the floor.
Change the safe thing every round, and let your kid name it every other round.

tiptoe-tag.title: Tiptoe Tag
tiptoe-tag.blurb: Good for a chase in a small room, where only toes may touch the floor and a heel means a freeze.
steps: Play tag where everyone may only move on tiptoe, chaser and runner alike.
Anyone whose heel touches the floor must freeze for three breaths before moving again.
Swap who chases at every tag, and stop the moment anyone says "stop".

sprint-and-settle.title: Sprint and Settle
sprint-and-settle.blurb: Good for a kid who needs to burn it off, and a parent who wants them calm straight afterwards.
steps: Run laps of the room together as fast as you can while you count them out loud.
On "settle", both drop to the floor, put a hand on your belly and take five slow breaths you can feel.
Jump up for another round, with one more lap each time and one more breath.

tree-pose-tag.title: Tree Pose Tag
tree-pose-tag.blurb: Good for a chase where the only safe place is standing on one leg like a tree.
steps: Chase your kid round the room, and they are safe whenever they stand still on one leg with arms up.
They can only hold the tree while you count to five, then they must run again.
Swap, and when you are the tree, your kid counts you down.

musical-cushion.title: Musical Cushion
musical-cushion.blurb: Good for one cushion, a song you can pause, and a kid who wants to beat you to the seat.
steps: Put one cushion in the middle and dance round it while a song plays.
Pause the song at any moment, and both of you race to sit on the cushion.
The loser picks the next song and does the pausing.

airplane-airports.title: Airplane Airports
airplane-airports.blurb: Good for a kid who still fits in your arms and a parent with one flight left in their back.
steps: Your kid names three airports in the room in order, like "the sofa, the door, the big chair".
Lift them as an airplane and fly to each one in that order, with them calling the next stop out loud.
Land on the sofa, then you fly on foot to three airports they call in a row.

sack-of-potatoes.title: Sack of Potatoes
sack-of-potatoes.blurb: Good for a floppy kid, a strong back, and a trip to the pretend shop that fails every time they giggle.
steps: Lift your kid over your shoulder as a sack of potatoes, which is floppy and silent.
Carry them to the shop across the room, and a wriggle or giggle means a soft drop onto the sofa and a restart.
Next trip they are a sack of jumping beans that must wriggle the whole way.

act-it-out.title: Act It Out
act-it-out.blurb: Good for a made up story where every line gets acted at once, by both of you.
steps: Tell one line of a story, like "the fox ran three times round the table", and you both act it at once.
Your kid tells the next line and you both act that, and so on, taking turns.
At the end, run the whole story again from the first line without the words.

bear-hunt-rewind.title: Bear Hunt Rewind
bear-hunt-rewind.blurb: Good for a march through grass, mud and a cave, then the same way back at double speed.
steps: Go on a bear hunt round the room, through long grass, thick mud and a dark cave, with a sound for each.
Find the bear behind the sofa, then run the whole way back doing the places in reverse order.
Next time add a new place, and the rewind has to include it too.

cushion-blueprint.title: Cushion Blueprint
cushion-blueprint.blurb: Good for a kid who draws, a pile of cushions, and a den built exactly as drawn.
steps: Your kid draws the den with a crayon, showing where each cushion goes.
Together carry and stack the cushions to match the drawing, checking it after every one.
Climb in, then they draw a second den and you build it alone while they check.

glued-to-the-floor.title: Glued to the Floor
glued-to-the-floor.blurb: Good for a kid who moves in strange ways, when one body part is stuck to the floor.
steps: Call a body part, like "one knee", and everyone crosses the room keeping that part on the floor.
Call a new part, like "a hand", halfway across, and the crossing continues with the new part glued.
Let your kid call the parts for you, and expect "bottom".

one-move-behind.title: One Move Behind
one-move-behind.blurb: Good for a dance where your kid copies not what you do, but what you did just before.
steps: Dance slowly to a song, changing move every few beats, while your kid watches.
They copy you one move late, so when you start a new move they do your old one.
Slow down whenever it breaks, and swap after a song.

dont-copy-me.title: Don't Copy Me
dont-copy-me.blurb: Good for a kid who copies everything, and a game where copying is the one thing you cannot do.
steps: Face each other, and every time you do a move, your kid must do any move except that one.
Do them faster, with big obvious moves like star jumps, which are the hardest not to copy.
Swap, and whoever copies by accident is the next leader.

ball-stopper.title: Ball Stopper
ball-stopper.blurb: Good for a hallway, a soft ball, and a kid who has to stop it with whatever body part you shout.
steps: Roll the ball down the hallway and, as it goes, shout a body part like "knee" or "elbow".
Your kid chases the ball and stops it with only that part, then rolls it back to you.
Shout later each time so they have to decide at the last second, then swap roles.

laser-limbo.title: Laser Limbo
laser-limbo.blurb: Good for two chairs, a scarf, and a spy who has to get under the laser without a sound.
steps: Hang a scarf between two chair backs as a laser beam and crawl under it one at a time.
If anyone touches the scarf, the alarm goes off, so they tiptoe back and try again.
After each clean crawl, lower the scarf a little, until it is a wriggle on your belly.

giant-steps.title: Giant Steps
giant-steps.blurb: Good for a hallway and a kid who can ask for giant steps but has to take whatever they are given.
steps: Stand at the far end while your kid asks, like "may I take three giant steps?"
Answer "yes" sometimes, and other times "no, take two bunny hops", and they do exactly that.
When they reach you, swap places and ask for the silliest steps you can think of.

sleeping-snake.title: Sleeping Snake
sleeping-snake.blurb: Good for a scarf, a wiggling parent on the floor, and a kid who jumps every time it slithers past.
steps: Lie on the floor and wiggle a scarf along the carpet like a snake while your kid jumps over it.
When the snake stops, it is asleep, and your kid must freeze until it slithers again.
Make the snake faster and the sleeps longer, then give your kid the snake and you jump.

safe-word-tag.title: Safe Word Tag
safe-word-tag.blurb: Good for a chase with a magic word that saves you, but only three times, so spend it wisely.
steps: Pick a silly safe word together, like "banana", and start a game of tag round the room.
Shouting the word freezes the chaser for a count of three, but each runner gets only three shouts a round.
Swap chaser at every tag, and count the shouts out loud on your fingers.

sneeze-freeze.title: Sneeze Freeze
sneeze-freeze.blurb: Good for a dance party with one real freeze signal hidden among lots of fake ones.
steps: Dance to a song, and the only thing that means freeze is your sneeze, a big loud "achoo".
Shout "freeze", clap and stamp as fakes, and your kid must keep dancing straight through them.
Swap, and pick a new secret signal each round, like a cough or a moo.

stop-on-the-sock.title: Stop on the Sock
stop-on-the-sock.blurb: Good for a hallway sprinter who needs some practice at the brakes.
steps: Lay a sock across the hallway and sprint at it from the far end.
Stop with your toes touching the sock, not a step past, and freeze there for a count of three.
Move the sock closer to the start each round, so the sprint gets shorter and the stop gets harder.

towel-dance.title: Towel Dance
towel-dance.blurb: Good for a wild dancer, a bath towel, and a song that keeps both feet on the towel.
steps: Spread a towel on the floor, put a song on, and dance as wildly as you can with both feet on it.
Any foot off the towel means a freeze until the other dancer taps you back in.
Fold the towel in half for the next song, then in half again.

puppet-strings.title: Puppet Strings
puppet-strings.blurb: Good for a floppy puppet, a bossy puppeteer, and a parent who moves one arm at a time.
steps: You are a puppet on strings, and your kid pulls a pretend string on one arm, one leg or your head.
Move only the part they pull, and let everything else hang floppy and still.
Swap, and pull two strings at once to make them walk and wave across the room.

wolf-time.title: Wolf Time
wolf-time.blurb: Good for a hallway, a hungry wolf, and a kid who counts their steps until dinner time.
steps: You are the wolf facing the wall at the far end, and your kid asks "what time is it, wolf?"
Answer a number up to ten, and they take exactly that many steps towards you, counting out loud.
When they are close, answer "dinner time" and chase them back to the start, then swap wolves.

singing-monster.title: Singing Monster
singing-monster.blurb: Good for a kid who loves to sing and a monster who can only move while the song is going.
steps: You are a monster who can only creep towards your kid while they sing.
The moment they stop singing, you freeze, and they can tiptoe away to a new spot.
Catch them with a tickle if the song never stops, then swap monsters.

sock-pair-run.title: Sock Pair Run
sock-pair-run.blurb: Good for the odd sock pile, a scattered room, and a kid who can hold one sock in mind while they hunt.
steps: Split five pairs of socks, scatter one of each pair round the room and keep the other five in a pile.
Hold up one sock for three seconds, hide it behind your back, and your kid runs to find its pair.
Swap, and they hold up two socks at once for you.

loud-hands-quiet-feet.title: Loud Hands Quiet Feet
loud-hands-quiet-feet.blurb: Good for a stompy kid who has to march in total silence while clapping as loud as they can.
steps: March the hallway together with silent feet and the loudest claps you can manage.
Turn round and march back with stomping feet and silent hands held behind your back.
Call "swap" halfway along the hall, so loud and quiet change places mid step.

treasure-map-dash.title: Treasure Map Dash
treasure-map-dash.blurb: Good for a crayon, a hidden toy, and a kid who reads a scribbled map by running it.
steps: Hide a toy while your kid waits in the hallway, then draw the room with a crayon and an X where it is.
Hand them the map, and they run to the X, checking the map against the room out loud.
Swap, and follow their map exactly, even when the sofa is a square.

cushion-sandwich.title: Cushion Sandwich
cushion-sandwich.blurb: Good for a cushion squeezed between two bellies and a walk across the room with no hands allowed.
steps: Hold a cushion between your belly and your kid's belly, hands behind your backs.
Walk it together across the room without dropping it, and a drop means back to the start.
Try it back to back next, then with two cushions.

who-moved-it.title: Who Moved It
who-moved-it.blurb: Good for a room your kid has to photograph in their head before they run to touch what changed.
steps: Lay out five things, like cushions and toys, and your kid looks at them hard for ten counts.
They turn to face the wall while you move one thing, then they turn back and run to touch it.
Move two things once they are good, and let them set the room for you.

parcel-delivery.title: Parcel Delivery
parcel-delivery.blurb: Good for a kid who wants to be carried, now as a parcel who must catch the truck's wrong turns.
steps: Your kid is a parcel who says the address out loud, like "under the table", and you are the truck.
Lift them and drive round the room, taking wrong turns on purpose until they shout "wrong way".
Deliver them to the address with a doorbell sound, then they drive a cushion parcel for you.

clap-then-catch.title: Clap Then Catch
clap-then-catch.blurb: Good for a scarf that falls slowly and a kid whose hands want to grab before the clap.
steps: Throw a scarf high and your kid must clap once before catching it.
Add a clap each round, two then three, so they have to wait while it floats down.
Swap, and let them call how many claps you owe before your catch.

rest-stop-chase.title: Rest Stop Chase
rest-stop-chase.blurb: Good for a chase that is fair, where the runner must rest and the chaser is stuck in slow motion.
steps: Spread cushions as rest stops, and the runner must sit on every one they pass for a count of three.
You chase in slow motion only, giant slow steps and a slow motion roar.
Swap after a catch, and the slow motion chaser is not allowed to speed up even to win.

exactly-ten-steps.title: Exactly Ten Steps
exactly-ten-steps.blurb: Good for a kid who sprints to the sofa, now having to get there in exactly ten steps, no more, no fewer.
steps: Walk from the door to the sofa in exactly ten steps, counting out loud and landing on ten.
Now do it in exactly four giant steps, then exactly twenty tiny ones.
Let your kid pick the number and the target, and watch each other for sneaky half steps.

moving-island.title: Moving Island
moving-island.blurb: Good for a kid who needs a proper chase and a parent with one lap of the living room in them.
steps: You are the sea monster, and the only safe island is the thing you call, like "the rug".
Chase your kid, and every few seconds call a new island, so the old one sinks and they must run for it.
A tag on the sea, or a kid still standing on a sunk island, means you swap and they are the monster.

change-of-plan.title: Change of Plan
change-of-plan.blurb: Good for a long hallway, a kid with a full tank, and a parent who can still turn fast.
steps: Shout a place, like "the door", and your kid sprints for it.
Before they arrive shout a new place, like "the sofa", and they turn on the spot and go for that.
A run only ends on a place you did not change, then your kid calls and you do the running.

shape-shifter.title: Shape Shifter
shape-shifter.blurb: Good for a kid who has run out of obstacle courses and a parent happy to be the course.
steps: Show two shapes first: a bridge on all fours to crawl under, and legs out straight as a log to jump over.
A tall wall with arms up is for running round, and you change shape without warning every few seconds.
Your kid must pick the right move for whatever shape you are now, then you swap and they shift.

dance-recipe.title: Dance Recipe
dance-recipe.blurb: Good for one song, a kid who loves a boogie, and a parent who can hold three moves in their head.
steps: Before the song, agree three moves in order, like a star jump, a crouch and a wiggle, and try them once.
Put the song on and both dance any way you like, as wild as you can.
When the song stops, your kid must do the three moves in the right order, then they pick three for you.

ghost-socks.title: Ghost Socks
ghost-socks.blurb: Good for a hallway, three odd socks, and a kid who thinks they never forget anything.
steps: Lay three socks along the hallway at odd distances and let your kid look hard for a count of five.
Pick the socks up, and your kid jumps to land exactly where each sock was, one jump per ghost sock.
Drop each sock back after their jump to check, then it is your turn to jump the ghosts.

hands-peekaboo.title: Hände-Kuckuck
hands-peekaboo.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deiner Brust, dich flach auf dem Rücken und freie Hände.
steps: Leg dich auf den Rücken, dein Baby auf der Brust, und versteck dein Gesicht hinter beiden Händen.
Halt still, zähl langsam bis drei, dann sag „Kuckuck!“ und mach die Hände weit auf.
Zähl jedes Mal ein bisschen länger und hör auf, solange dein Baby noch lächelt.

cloth-on-your-face.title: Wo bin ich hin?
cloth-on-your-face.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten, das schon greift – das Tuch liegt auf deinem Gesicht, nie auf seinem.
steps: Leg dich neben dein Baby und leg dir ein Tuch oder Handtuch übers Gesicht.
Frag „Wo bin ich hin?“ und warte, bis es das Tuch wegzieht, oder zähl langsam bis fünf und schau selbst hervor.
Sag mit breitem Grinsen „Da bin ich!“ und spiel weiter, solange es Lust hat.

under-the-cup.title: Unterm Becher
under-the-cup.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten, das schon nach Dingen greift, und dich auf dem Boden daneben.
steps: Stülp einen Becher über ein Spielzeug, während dein Baby zusieht, wie es verschwindet.
Frag „Wo ist es hin?“ und warte einen langen Atemzug, bevor du den Becher berührst.
Heb ihn staunend hoch, stülp ihn wieder drüber und lass jetzt dein Baby heben.

sock-puppet-chat.title: Plausch mit der Sockenpuppe
sock-puppet-chat.blurb: Gut für dich, platt auf dem Sofa, eine einzelne Socke und ein Baby, das gern angeplaudert wird.
steps: Zieh dir eine Socke über die Hand, lass sie über dein Knie zu deinem Baby linsen und sag mit Piepsstimme „Hallo“.
Lass die Puppe abtauchen und warte still, bis dein Baby irgendeinen Laut macht.
Lass sie woanders wieder auftauchen und antworten – so geht das Gespräch hin und her.

toy-comet.title: Spielzeug-Komet
toy-comet.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 5 Monaten, ihr beide auf dem Rücken, mit einem Spielzeug und ohne Termine.
steps: Halt ein Spielzeug etwa eine Unterarmlänge vor das Gesicht deines Babys, bis sein Blick daran hängen bleibt.
Lass es langsam zur Seite gleiten, halt an und warte, bis die Augen nachkommen, bevor du weitermachst.
Wechsel ab und zu die Richtung und hör auf, wenn dein Baby wegschaut.

cushion-tunnel-toy.title: Kissentunnel
cushion-tunnel-toy.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 5 Monaten, das genau hinschaut, und dich mit einem Kissen auf dem Boden.
steps: Stell ein Kissen aufrecht zwischen dich und dein Baby und lass ein Spielzeug langsam dahinter entlanglaufen.
Warte kurz, solange es versteckt ist, lass es dann auf der anderen Seite herauskommen und sag seinen Namen.
Schaut dein Baby schon zur anderen Seite, bevor das Spielzeug auftaucht, schick es denselben Weg zurück.

follow-their-gaze.title: Wo guckst du hin?
follow-their-gaze.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deiner Brust oder neben dir, das sich in einem Zimmer umschaut, das du heute nicht mehr aufräumst.
steps: Beobachte die Augen deines Babys und schau dahin, wo sie landen, auch wenn es die Decke ist.
Benenne es mit ein paar warmen Worten wie „die Lampe, die gelbe Lampe“ und schau weiter mit hin.
Sag nichts mehr, bis die Augen weiterwandern, und folge ihnen dann zum nächsten Ding.

babble-back.title: Brabbel-Echo
babble-back.blurb: Gut für ein gesprächiges Baby ab etwa 3 Monaten und dich, wenn du noch reden, aber nicht mehr aufstehen kannst.
steps: Warte, bis dein Baby irgendeinen Laut macht, und antworte, als wäre es ein echter Satz.
Halt inne, schau es an und lass ihm eine lange Pause, damit es antworten kann.
Halt das Hin und Her in Gang und lass dein Baby das Gespräch beenden, wenn es wegschaut.

missing-last-word.title: Das fehlende Wort
missing-last-word.blurb: Gut für ein Lied, das dein Baby schon hundertmal gehört hat, gesungen im Liegen bei gedämpftem Licht.
steps: Sing langsam ein Lied, das dein Baby gut kennt, und schau ihm dabei ins Gesicht.
Hör kurz vor dem letzten Wort einer Zeile auf und halt die Stille mit hochgezogenen Augenbrauen.
Warte, bis es zappelt, strampelt oder dich anschaut, dann sing das Wort mit einem breiten Lächeln.

lullaby-stop-start.title: Schlaflied mit Pause
lullaby-stop-start.blurb: Gut für die ruhigen Minuten vor dem Schlafen, dein Baby auf deiner Brust und das Licht gedimmt.
steps: Leg dich auf den Rücken, dein Baby auf der Brust, und summ oder sing ein Schlaflied, das es kennt.
Hör mitten in einer Zeile auf, werd ganz still und atme langsam.
Sobald es zappelt, gurrt oder hochschaut, sing an der Stelle weiter, wo du aufgehört hast.

copy-cat-faces.title: Grimassen-Echo
copy-cat-faces.blurb: Gut für eine Runde Gesicht an Gesicht ab etwa 6 Monaten, dein Baby auf deiner Brust oder neben dir, ganz ohne Spielzeug.
steps: Mach Gesicht oder Laut deines Babys einen Wimpernschlag später nach, ob Zunge rausstrecken, Quietschen oder Stirnrunzeln.
Mach das ein paar Mal, dann zieh langsam selbst eine neue Grimasse und halt sie.
Halt die Grimasse und warte, bis dein Baby versucht, sie nachzumachen.

little-piggy-pause.title: Zehenvers mit Pause
little-piggy-pause.blurb: Gut für nackte Füße auf deinem Schoß, ein Baby auf dem Rücken und dich, wenn du einen Kinderreim kennst.
steps: Sag „Das ist der Daumen“ langsam an den Zehen deines Babys auf, eine Zeile pro Zeh.
Mach beim letzten Zeh eine Pause und halt den Fuß ruhig, während du langsam bis drei zählst.
Dann lass bei „und der Kleine isst sie alle auf“ die Finger zum Bauch hochlaufen und mach am anderen Fuß weiter.

round-the-garden.title: Kommt eine Maus
round-the-garden.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß mit offener Hand und dich, wenn deine Hände nach dem Tag noch mitmachen.
steps: Sag „Kommt eine Maus, baut ein Haus“ auf und lass deinen Finger in der offenen Hand deines Babys kreisen.
Bei „kommt eine Mücke, baut eine Brücke“ lass die Finger den Arm hochkrabbeln und halt knapp unter dem Kinn inne.
Warte, bis es sich windet, kitzel bei „kommt ein Floh, der macht so“ einmal ganz sanft unterm Kinn und hör auf, wenn es sich wegdreht.

floor-mirror-faces.title: Wer ist da drin?
floor-mirror-faces.blurb: Gut für die Bauchlage ab etwa 5 Monaten, du flach neben deinem Baby und ein Spiegel vor euch.
steps: Leg dich neben dein Baby auf den Bauch und stell einen Spiegel so auf, dass ihr beide darin zu sehen seid.
Tipp auf das Baby im Spiegel und sag seinen Namen, dann tipp auf seine echte Nase und sag ihn noch mal.
Mach langsam ein Gesicht in den Spiegel und schau, ob es sich zu deinem Spiegelbild oder zu dir dreht.

ready-steady-raspberry.title: Achtung, fertig, prusten!
ready-steady-raspberry.blurb: Gut für einen nackten Bauch, ein Baby quer auf deinem Schoß oder neben dir und dich mit dem letzten Rest Puste.
steps: Sag „Achtung“, warte, sag „fertig“, warte länger, dann „los“ und prust ganz sanft auf seinen Bauch.
Prust, bis du „Stopp“ sagst, dann heb den Kopf und halt still, während du bis zwei zählst.
Mach erst weiter, wenn es dich anschaut oder strampelt, und zieh die Pausen in die Länge, sobald es den Dreh raushat.

baby-mind-reader.title: Gedankenleser
baby-mind-reader.blurb: Gut für ein quengeliges oder zappeliges Baby auf deinem Schoß und dich, wenn du nur noch leise reden kannst.
steps: Beobachte dein Baby kurz und sag, was es zu wollen scheint, etwa „du willst den Löffel“.
Benenne auch das Gefühl, ganz ruhig, etwa „das Geräusch hat dich erschreckt“.
Mach nach jeder Vermutung eine Pause, gib ihm einen Moment zum Antworten und hilf ihm dann mit dem, was es wollte.

lamp-off-lamp-on.title: Licht aus, Licht an
lamp-off-lamp-on.blurb: Gut fürs Sofa neben einer Lampe in der Dämmerung, dein Baby auf dem Schoß und deine freie Hand am Schalter.
steps: Setz dich mit deinem Baby auf dem Schoß neben eine Lampe in Reichweite oder leuchte mit der Handytaschenlampe an die Decke.
Sag langsam „aus“ und schalt sie aus, warte, bis es danach sucht, dann sag „an“ und hol das Licht zurück.
Mach die dunkle Pause jedes Mal ein bisschen länger und sprich die ganze Zeit leise.

wheres-your-nose.title: Wo ist deine Nase?
wheres-your-nose.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß, das zu dir hochschaut, und dich mit Energie für genau einen Finger.
steps: Frag „Wo ist deine Nase?“ und warte einen langen Atemzug, während du ihm ins Gesicht schaust.
Tipp sanft auf seine Nase und sag „Nase“, dann genauso bei Ohren, Zehen und Bauch.
Frag nach ein paar Runden „Wo ist meine Nase?“ und führ seine Hand zu deiner.

flat-out-story.title: Bilderbuch im Liegen
flat-out-story.blurb: Gut fürs Bett, dein Baby neben dir, ein Bilderbuch und keine Kraft mehr für verstellte Stimmen.
steps: Leg dich neben dein Baby und halt ein aufgeschlagenes Bilderbuch über euch beide.
Zeig auf ein Bild, benenne es und warte, bis die Augen deines Babys darauf landen, bevor du umblätterst oder weiterredest.
Schaut es auf etwas anderes auf der Seite, benenne lieber das und bleib dort.

slow-fist-open.title: Die langsame Faust
slow-fist-open.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 5 Monaten, das schon greift, und dich mit einer freien Hand.
steps: Schließ vor den Augen deines Babys die Faust um ein Spielzeug, das zu groß zum Verschlucken ist, sodass ein Stück rausschaut.
Frag „Was ist da drin?“ und öffne einen Finger nach dem anderen, so langsam du kannst.
Lass es deine Finger aufziehen, wenn es mag, und mach die Faust für eine neue Runde wieder zu.

sock-foot-vanish.title: Zappelsocke
sock-foot-vanish.blurb: Gut für dich flach auf dem Teppich, ein Baby von etwa 6 Monaten an deinen Füßen und eine bunte Socke.
steps: Leg dich mit einer Socke an einem Fuß auf den Teppich und wackel mit den Zehen, bis dein Baby hinschaut.
Schieb den Sockenfuß unter eine Decke und flüster: „Wo ist die Socke hin?“
Wackel unter der Decke mit dem Fuß, warte und lass dein Baby die Decke wegziehen, um die Socke zu finden.

something-moves.title: Da bewegt sich was
something-moves.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 5 Monaten auf deiner Brust und ein Zimmer, in dem ein Ventilator oder Vorhang die Arbeit macht.
steps: Leg dich mit deinem Baby hin und such etwas, das sich von selbst bewegt, etwa einen Ventilator, einen Vorhang oder einen Schatten.
Dreht euch so, dass ihr es beide seht, und schaut es wortlos zusammen an, bis dein Baby wegschaut.
Wenn es hinschaut, sag leise etwas dazu, etwa „rundherum“, und sei wieder still.

tummy-time-name.title: Gesicht gefunden!
tummy-time-name.blurb: Gut für die Bauchlage ab etwa 5 Monaten, du auch auf dem Bauch, Nase an Nase auf dem Teppich.
steps: Leg dich auf den Bauch, eine Handlänge vor deinem Baby, und sei still, bis es wegschaut.
Sag einmal leise seinen Namen und warte, bis sein Blick zu deinem Gesicht zurückkommt.
Wenn es dich findet, halt den Blick mit einem großen, langsamen Lächeln und erzähl ihm eine Sache von seinem Tag.

toy-give-back.title: Bitte schön
toy-give-back.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 9 Monaten auf deinem Schoß und dich, wenn du noch eine Hand ausstrecken kannst.
steps: Gib deinem Baby ein Spielzeug, sag „bitte schön“ und lass es eine Weile damit spielen.
Halt deine offene Hand hin, sag „ich bin dran“ und warte, ohne zu greifen, auch wenn es eine Minute dauert.
Legt es dir das Spielzeug in die Hand, sag „danke“ und gib es gleich zurück mit „du bist dran“.

eyes-on-me.title: Schau mich an
eyes-on-me.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten neben dir, ein Spielzeug in deiner Hand und dein Gesicht als Hauptattraktion.
steps: Leg dich Gesicht an Gesicht zu deinem Baby und summ, während dein Gesicht langsam Quatsch macht.
Wackel ab und zu kurz mit einem Spielzeug am Rand seines Blickfelds und versteck es dann wieder.
Bleiben seine Augen bei dir statt beim Spielzeug, belohn es mit einem riesigen Grinsen und einem Kuss.

look-where-i-look.title: Folg meinem Blick
look-where-i-look.blurb: Gut für ein Baby von etwa 9 Monaten, das schon sitzt, zwei Spielsachen auf dem Teppich und dich, wenn du nur noch den Kopf bewegen kannst.
steps: Setz dich zu deinem Baby und leg zwei Spielsachen vor euch auf den Boden.
Dreh den Kopf zu einem Spielzeug, schau es ganz genau an und sag einmal, wie es heißt.
Warte, bis seine Augen deinem Blick folgen, dann sag den Namen noch mal und gib es ihm.

uh-oh-cup.title: Hoppla, Becher!
uh-oh-cup.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 5 Monaten neben dir, einen leeren Becher und dich, wenn du noch den Kopf neigen kannst.
steps: Leg dich neben dein Baby, balancier einen leeren Becher auf der Stirn und zähl langsam „eins, zwei, drei“.
Neig den Kopf von deinem Baby weg, sodass der Becher mit einem lauten „Hoppla“ auf den Teppich rutscht.
Stell ihn wieder auf und zähl noch mal, jedes Mal etwas langsamer, und schau, wie es schon vor dem Fallen gespannt wartet.

snore-and-wake.title: Schnarchbär
snore-and-wake.blurb: Gut für dich, wenn du die Augen zumachen willst, und ein Baby von etwa 6 Monaten, das neben dir sitzt oder liegt.
steps: Leg dich auf den Teppich, mach die Augen zu und schnarch laut, eine Hand an deinem Baby.
Sobald es dich berührt oder einen Laut macht, wach langsam und überrascht auf und sag „Oh, hallo“.
Lächle, gähn, mach die Augen wieder zu und schnarch weiter, damit es noch mal probieren kann.

pick-one-toy.title: Such dir eins aus
pick-one-toy.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten, das schon greift, auf deinem Schoß oder neben dir, mit zwei Spielsachen in Reichweite.
steps: Halt zwei Spielsachen hoch, in jeder Hand eins, ein Stück auseinander und gut erreichbar.
Frag „Welches?“ und warte reglos, bis es eins länger anschaut oder danach greift.
Gib ihm das, sag, wie es heißt, und leg das andere weg, bevor du wieder zwei anbietest.

house-sounds.title: Was war das?
house-sounds.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deiner Brust am Abend, während das Haus seine üblichen Geräusche macht.
steps: Lieg mit deinem Baby still da und warte auf ein Geräusch, etwa den Wasserkocher, eine Tür oder einen Hund draußen.
Frag „Was war das?“ und dreh den Kopf langsam dorthin, damit es sich mitdreht.
Benenne es mit zwei, drei Wörtern, dann seid wieder still und wartet zusammen auf das nächste.

scarf-tug-turns.title: Zieh mal!
scarf-tug-turns.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten, das fest greift, auf deinem Schoß, mit einem Schal oder Geschirrtuch.
steps: Lass dein Baby ein Ende eines Schals greifen, während du das andere hältst.
Sag „ich bin dran“ und zieh einmal sanft, dann lass locker und sag „du bist dran“.
Warte auf sein Ziehen, bevor du wieder ziehst, und lass es am Ende den Schal gewinnen.

peeking-tail.title: Da guckt was raus
peeking-tail.blurb: Gut für ein Baby von etwa 5 Monaten neben dir, das schon greift, aber ein ganz verstecktes Spielzeug noch nicht findet.
steps: Leg ein Tuch so über ein Spielzeug, dass eine Ecke noch rausschaut, genau in Reichweite deines Babys.
Frag „Wo ist es hin?“, tipp auf das Stück, das rausguckt, und nimm die Hände weg.
Zieht es das Tuch weg, freu dich leise mit und deck das Spielzeug jedes Mal ein bisschen mehr zu.

two-hands-full.title: Beide Hände voll
two-hands-full.blurb: Gut für ein Baby von etwa einem Jahr mit einem Spielzeug in jeder Hand und dich, wenn du warten kannst.
steps: Warte, bis dein Baby in jeder Hand ein Spielzeug hat, und halt ihm ein drittes hin, das es mag.
Sag nichts und zähl langsam bis zehn, während es überlegt, was es tun soll.
Egal, was es versucht, ob es eins fallen lässt oder trotzdem zugreift, sag liebevoll, was es tut, und biete das neue Spielzeug noch mal an.

empty-cup-tea.title: Teeparty
empty-cup-tea.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 10 Monaten auf deinem Schoß, einen leeren Becher und dich, wenn du noch laut schlürfen kannst.
steps: Heb einen leeren Becher an die Lippen und trink laut daraus, mit einem großen „Aaah“ am Ende.
Halt deinem Baby den Becher an den Mund, als würde es trinken, dann gib ihn ihm und warte.
Was es auch damit macht, schlürf mit und sag „Prost“.

row-boat-stop.title: Schaukelboot
row-boat-stop.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby auf deinem Schoß, ein Lied, das ihr beide kennt, und dich, wenn du schaukeln, aber nicht aufstehen kannst.
steps: Setz dein Baby dir zugewandt auf den Schoß, halt seine Hände und schaukel vor und zurück, während du „Alle meine Entchen“ singst.
Hör irgendwo mitten im Lied schlagartig auf, nie zweimal an derselben Stelle, halt die Hände still und bleib ganz ruhig.
Sobald es sich vorlehnt, zieht oder strampelt, schaukel weiter und sing das Lied zu Ende.

patacake-pause.title: Backe, backe Kuchen
patacake-pause.blurb: Gut für ein Baby, das dir gegenübersitzt und den Reim schon liebt, und Hände, die ihn auswendig können.
steps: Setzt euch gegenüber und sag „Backe, backe Kuchen“ auf, bei jedem Takt klatschst du sanft in die Händchen deines Babys.
Mach vor dem großen Klatscher die Hände weit auf und erstarr einen langen Atemzug lang.
Klatsch, sobald seine Augen zu deinen hochkommen, und mach die Pause in der nächsten Runde etwas länger.

trot-to-boston.title: Hoppe, hoppe Reiter
trot-to-boston.blurb: Gut für ein Baby, das gut auf deinen Knien sitzt, wenn du es unter den Armen hältst, und dich auf einem Stuhl.
steps: Setz dein Baby dir zugewandt auf die Knie, halt es fest unter den Armen und lass es zu „Hoppe, hoppe Reiter“ hüpfen.
Mach bei „plumps“ die Knie auseinander, sodass es eine Handbreit absackt, und halt es dabei die ganze Zeit fest.
Sprich die letzte Zeile jede Runde etwas langsamer und schau, wie es sich schon vor dem Plumps anspannt.

two-cup-switch.title: Becher-Tausch
two-cup-switch.blurb: Gut fürs Hochstuhl-Tablett und ein Baby ab etwa 8 Monaten, das nach allem greift, was du versteckst.
steps: Stell zwei Becher umgedreht aufs Tablett und versteck ein Spielzeug unter einem, während dein Baby zusieht.
Zähl langsam „eins, zwei, drei“, dann lass es einen Becher hochheben und das Spielzeug finden.
Leg das Spielzeug nach ein paar Treffern sichtbar unter den anderen Becher, zähl wieder und schau, wohin es greift.

drop-and-tip.title: Rein und raus
drop-and-tip.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby, das alles fallen lässt, und dich mit einem Becher und sonst nichts.
steps: Halt einen hohen Becher tief vor dein Baby und lass es einen Baustein oder eine eingerollte Socke reinfallen.
Schüttel ihn einmal, damit es das hört, frag „Wo ist es hin?“ und warte, bis es zum Becher schaut.
Kipp ihn langsam in seinen Schoß aus, gib den Baustein zurück und halt den Becher jede Runde etwas höher.

knock-on-three.title: Eins, zwei, bumm!
knock-on-three.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby, das jeden Turm umhaut, und dich mit genug Bechern.
steps: Stapel drei oder vier Becher, während dein Baby zusieht, und nimm dann seine Hände locker in deine.
Zähl langsam „eins, zwei“ und lass seine Hände erst bei „drei“ los, damit es den Turm umhauen kann.
Bau neu und mach die Pause vor „drei“ jedes Mal ein kleines bisschen länger.

ball-back.title: Ball hin, Ball her
ball-back.blurb: Gut für ein Baby, das sicher auf dem Boden sitzt oder krabbelt, und dich ihm gegenüber.
steps: Setz dich deinem Baby gegenüber auf den Boden, die Beine gegrätscht wie ein kleines Gehege, und roll den Ball langsam in seinen Schoß.
Streck die Hände aus und warte still, bis es ihn zurückschubst oder damit herkrabbelt.
Sag „ich bin dran“, roll ihn wieder hin und lass die Pausen länger werden.

thank-you-swap.title: Danke, bitte
thank-you-swap.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby, das dir Sachen reicht und sie sofort zurückwill.
steps: Halt deine offene Hand hin und warte, bis dein Baby das Spielzeug hineinlegt, dann sag „danke“.
Behalt es einen Moment, biete es zurück an und lass erst los, wenn sich seine Hand darum schließt.
Nimm ein zweites Spielzeug dazu, damit es eins loslassen muss, um das andere zu nehmen.

sock-drop-look.title: Socke fällt
sock-drop-look.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß am Tisch oder ein Krabbelkind, das gern hinterherkrabbelt.
steps: Halt eine eingerollte Socke auf Augenhöhe deines Babys, sag „Achtung“ und lass sie fallen.
Schaut zusammen auf den Boden und frag „Wo ist sie hin?“, bevor du hinzeigst.
Lass es die Socke entdecken oder hinkrabbeln, dann heb sie auf und lass sie noch mal fallen.

book-where-dog.title: Wo ist der Hund?
book-where-dog.blurb: Gut für ein Bilderbuch, ein Baby auf deinem Schoß und dieselbe Seite zum zwanzigsten Mal.
steps: Schlag ein Bilderbuch auf deinem Schoß auf und tipp auf eine Sache auf der Seite, während du sie benennst.
Blätter um und wieder zurück, frag „Wo ist der Hund?“ und warte, bevor du zeigst.
Benenne, worauf es tippt, auch wenn es nicht der Hund ist, und frag dann noch mal.

switch-boss.title: Chef am Schalter
switch-boss.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deiner Hüfte am Lichtschalter, wenn es im Zimmer dunkel wird.
steps: Stell dich mit deinem Baby auf der Hüfte an den Schalter, mach das Licht an und sag „an“.
Leg die Hand auf den Schalter und warte, bis es quietscht, strampelt oder hinstarrt, dann drück und sag „aus“.
Sag dabei, was es sich gewünscht hat, etwa „du willst das Licht an“, und schalt nur auf sein Zeichen.

sock-fist.title: Welche Hand?
sock-fist.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 8 Monaten, das schon greift, und dich mit zwei Händen und einer Socke.
steps: Zeig deinem Baby eine zusammengeknüllte Socke, schließ die Faust darum und halt beide Fäuste nebeneinander hin.
Frag „Welche Hand?“ und zähl langsam bis zwei, bevor es wählen darf.
Öffne die Faust, nach der es greift, egal welche, und wechsel jede Runde die Hand.

half-hidden-toy.title: Halb versteckt
half-hidden-toy.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby ab etwa 6 Monaten, das schon greift, ein Lieblingsspielzeug und ein Geschirrtuch.
steps: Stell das Spielzeug vor dein Baby und leg vor seinen Augen ein Tuch über die Hälfte.
Frag „Wo ist es hin?“ und warte, bis es am Tuch zieht oder das Spielzeug packt.
Klappt das leicht, deck es ganz zu, warte einen langen Atemzug und frag noch mal.

copy-cat-hands.title: Klatsch zurück
copy-cat-hands.blurb: Gut für ein Baby, das dir gegenübersitzt und gerade anfängt zu klatschen oder zu winken.
steps: Klatsch zweimal langsam vor deinem Baby, dann halt die Hände still hoch und warte.
Klatscht es oder versucht es, klatsch einmal zurück und wechsel zum Winken.
Fängt es eine eigene Bewegung an, mach sie genau nach und lass es eine Weile führen.

big-tiny-voice.title: Laut und leise
big-tiny-voice.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß und ein Lied, das es schon hundertmal gehört hat.
steps: Sing eine Zeile eines Liedes, das es kennt, mit deiner lautesten Stimme, die Arme weit ausgebreitet.
Sing die nächste Zeile im Flüsterton, ganz nah, damit es auf deinen Mund schaut.
Spring immer weiter zwischen laut und leise hin und her und wechsle schon früher, sobald seine Augen zu deinen hochkommen.

point-and-name.title: Zeigen und benennen
point-and-name.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß in jedem Zimmer, ab etwa 9 Monaten, wenn es anfängt, einem Zeigefinger zu folgen.
steps: Zeig auf eine Sache im Zimmer und halt den Arm dort, bis die Augen deines Babys darauf landen.
Benenne sie einmal langsam, dann schau wieder zu deinem Baby und warte.
Folg jetzt umgekehrt seinem Blick und benenne alles, was es anstarrt.

window-movers.title: Fenstergucker
window-movers.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deiner Hüfte am Fenster, während das Essen kocht oder der Tag ausklingt.
steps: Stell dich mit deinem Baby auf der Hüfte ans Fenster und warte wortlos, bis sich etwas bewegt.
Sobald es hinschaut, zeig darauf, sag, was es ist, etwa „ein Bus“, und schau mit ihm hinterher, bis er weg ist.
Sei wieder still und warte mit ihm auf das Nächste, das vorbeikommt.

up-up-down.title: Rauf, rauf, runter
up-up-down.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby auf deinen Schienbeinen und dich mit angewinkelten Knien auf dem Boden.
steps: Setz dich mit angewinkelten Knien auf den Boden, dein Baby dir zugewandt auf den Schienbeinen, deine Hände unter seinen Armen.
Sing bei jedem langsamen Anheben der Knie „rauf“ und „runter“, wenn du sie auf einmal senkst.
Ändere, wie oft es rauf geht, bevor es runter geht, und halt inne, wenn es schon vorher grinst.

ring-ring-phone.title: Telefon für dich
ring-ring-phone.blurb: Gut für ein Baby ab etwa 9 Monaten, das dein Handy anbrabbelt, im Hochstuhl oder auf dem Boden.
steps: Halt die Hand ans Ohr, sag „Ring, ring, hallo?“ und plauder kurz mit Oma.
Halt deine Hand an sein Ohr, sag „das ist für dich“ und warte auf irgendeinen Laut.
Antworte auf alles, was es sagt, und reich den Hörer dann hin und her.

shake-and-stop.title: Schüttel-Stopp
shake-and-stop.blurb: Gut für ein sitzendes Baby, einen Becher, eine eingerollte Socke und dich, wenn du noch summen kannst.
steps: Steck eine eingerollte Socke in einen Becher, halt die Hand oben drauf und schüttel ihn im Takt, während du singst.
Hör mitten in einer Zeile mit Schütteln und Singen auf, halt den Becher still und schau in sein Gesicht.
Fang wieder an, sobald es hochschaut oder strampelt, und lass es dann selbst den Becher halten und schütteln.

mirror-swap.title: Spiegelbaby
mirror-swap.blurb: Gut für ein Baby auf deinem Schoß vor einem Spiegel, sobald es das Baby darin anlächelt.
steps: Setz dich mit deinem Baby auf dem Schoß vor einen Spiegel und wink euch beiden im Spiegel zu.
